q52.headline: D-52 resolves cleanly, and CR-E05 §5's own hypothesis is refuted by the record: nothing changed in the Rule 1102 paperwork overnight. State's Exhibit 12.3 was the identical, unamended statement — and it already contained the "only changes are some zooms and red highlights" sentence on Day 1, which the State quoted aloud in argument before the exclusion. What changed was a NEW EXHIBIT: State's Exhibit 12.4, the same compilation with the circles, blurs and zooms stripped out, built overnight exactly as the State told the court on the Day 1 record it would ("our intent is to prepare an original version of the video that has been in dispute today without the circles, without the blur and without the zooming in ... introduce that tomorrow as a different exhibit"). 12.4 was admitted, played and broadcast; the witness then itemized every difference between 12.4 and 12.1 under oath; 12.1 was re-offered on "the foundation that was laid yesterday" and admitted. The precise defect the court named on Day 1 — no Rule 1102 statement from whoever MADE the alterations — was never literally cured; it was made immaterial by comparison. And the court never stated on the record why it was now satisfied.

findings.finding: THE ANSWER TO D-52. What changed in the foundation overnight was not a document but an exhibit. State's Exhibit 12.4 — described by the witness as "the same footage" as 12.1 but with "no circles or blurs" and no zooming — was prepared overnight by the Utah County Attorney's Office, reviewed by the witness on the morning of Day 2, offered first, and admitted (played in the courtroom and broadcast). Only after 12.4 was in evidence and had been narrated in full was 12.1 re-offered. The State had announced precisely this plan on the Day 1 record before adjourning.
findings.locator: day1.txt line 10859 (stream 07:42:11) and line 10883 (07:43:21); day2.txt lines 579-667, 812-820

findings.finding: State's Exhibit 12.3 was NOT amended, supplemented or replaced. On Day 2 it is treated throughout as already in evidence — "I believe that has actually been admitted into evidence as State's Exhibit 12.3" — displayed on the witness's monitor, and read from. The re-offer of 12.1 rests expressly on "the foundation that was laid yesterday, including the written statement from Mr. Olson, which has been admitted into evidence." No new or supplemental Rule 1102 statement was offered, marked or admitted at any point in the passage.

CR-E05 §5's HYPOTHESIS IS REFUTED. The sentence "The only changes are some zooms and red highlights, which were not part of the original recording" was already in the 12.3 that was admitted on Day 1. The State quoted that exact language in its Day 1 argument for admitting 12.1 — before the ruling — attributing it to the 12.3 already in evidence, and the court's own ruling shows it read 12.3 the same way ("Mr. Olson saying, 'This is the video, minus the alterations'"). CR-E05's inference that the Day-1 12.3 "evidently did not" address the alterations is contradicted by the Day-1 transcript itself.
findings.locator: day1.txt line 10021 (06:49:45) and line 10065 (06:53:46), against CR-E05 line 245

findings.finding: The premise underlying that hypothesis is also wrong. The Day-1 objection did not succeed because 12.3 was silent about the alterations; it succeeded because no Rule 1102 statement and no witness came from whoever MADE them. The court: "you don't have a person testifying 1102 saying, 'I made the alterations'" and "I'm missing a link." Describing an alteration is not authenticating it — so CR-E05's reasoning ("or the objection could not have succeeded") is a non sequitur. The objection succeeded notwithstanding the description.

CR-E05 §5 is internally inconsistent, and the library already held the answer. The section's own narrative paragraph correctly records that "The State announced it would prepare and offer an unaltered version the next day," while the D-52 register row two paragraphs later hypothesises a revised Rule 1102 statement instead. CR-E04 §3's exhibit table also already listed 12.4 as "the same compilation without circles, blurs or zooming" — the resolving fact was sitting in two library files; what was missing was only the causal link between them.

The foundation actually supplied for 12.1 on Day 2, in order: (1) the 12.3 sentence read aloud from the already-admitted statement; (2) 12.4 admitted, published and broadcast; (3) the witness's sworn, itemized comparison of 12.1 against 12.4 — red ovals/circles as temporary overlays marking persons of interest, face-blurring confined to the parking-garage sequence and to faces only, zooming concentrated on the Losee-rooftop footage — each item followed by testimony that it did not change the content or accuracy of the video; (4) a re-offer resting on "the foundation that was laid yesterday."

The court did not state a basis for admitting 12.1. The ruling opens "Anything further from the parties as it relates to 12.1? All right, well I will admit 12.1 into evidence" and then addresses publication only. The renewed authenticity objection is not addressed anywhere on the record, and the Day-1 "missing link" is never mentioned again.

That 12.4 was the operative cure is an inference, not a stated holding — but a well-supported one. It rests on: the court itself having asked on Day 1 "do you have a version of this exhibit that does not have the zooming in or the circling?"; the State's on-record undertaking to build exactly that overnight; the sequencing on Day 2 (12.4 admitted and narrated first, 12.1 re-offered only afterward); and the court's own publication reasoning, which turns entirely on 12.1 and 12.4 being the same footage. Stated at Medium-high rather than High solely because the court never articulated it.

The objection was the same objection and was RENEWED, not abandoned: "We renew our authenticity objection and we also object for admission purposes. And then we also object to the publication for the same reasons, the fair trial issues that we raised with the unaltered version that was just submitted." This is distinct from the standing Rule 1102 / Article I §12 hearsay objection, which the court had formally noted that same morning as continuing so it need not be repeated.
findings.locator: day2.txt line 1780 (01:05:35); standing objection at lines 343-367 (00:17:51-00:20:05)

findings.finding: The Day-1 defect was never literally cured on the Day-2 record. Nobody from the Utah County Attorney's Office testified; no Rule 1102 statement from the person who made the alterations was offered; and the State's Day-1 offer — "We could actually call that person as a witness if that would cure that, and we're prepared to do that if necessary" — was not taken up in the Day-2 passage. The evidentiary gap the court identified was made immaterial by side-by-side comparison, not filled.

Publication terms. State's Exhibit 12.4: admitted, played in the courtroom, and expressly permitted to be broadcast by the media. State's Exhibit 12.1: admitted into evidence but NOT published in the courtroom and NOT broadcast; the court instead viewed the zoomed portion on the court's and counsel's monitors in open court, with the video's internal counter put on the record (started just before the six-minute mark; the court read the stop point as 6:23 and was corrected by the State to 8:23). The State's fallback request to publish only the roughly two-minute zoomed segment was objected to and denied. Counsel were cautioned to shield their own screens.

Rule 403 reasoning. The court raised Rule 403 sua sponte, directing counsel to "the last four words" — "needlessly presenting cumulative evidence" — read the whole rule aloud, and noted "I recognize there is no jury. I am the magistrate. I am the fact finder." The State argued the two videos are not cumulative because the enhanced one is legible where 12.4 is not. The court admitted 12.1 anyway, then used essentially the cumulativeness rationale to deny re-publication: it is "the exact same video, the difference being enhancements made," and "there is nothing on this video from what's been represented that the public hasn't already seen."

Structural observation: the sameness that carried admission is what defeated publication. 12.4 solved the authentication problem by demonstrating that 12.1 is the same footage; that same demonstration then made 12.1 needlessly cumulative to re-play. The State's own argument had to run in both directions at once — identical enough to authenticate, different enough to be worth showing.

The Day-2 non-publication ruling was NOT the end of the story, and no library file records the sequel. On Day 4, counsel appearing for the victim's family moved for reconsideration so the family could view 12.1 (the enhanced version), arguing that 12.4 "was very hard for the family to view"; the State did not oppose. On Day 5 the court adhered to that reconsidered ruling: 12.1 "may be viewed by all persons physically present in the courtroom, including victim representative Ms. Kirk," with the livestream temporarily limited to audio only and no still capture of any monitor — and 12.1 was then played.

Neither 12.1 nor 12.4 is the whole record. The witness testified 12.1 does not include all footage collected from UVU, nor all footage of the person he believes to be Robinson; and that there is additional campus footage not in 12.4. Selection — which footage was compiled in and which left out — is covered by no Rule 1102 statement anywhere in the passage, and 12.4 is itself a compilation prepared by the same office, not raw footage; its foundation was the witness's testimony that it "appear[s] to be identical to the raw footage" he had personally reviewed.

Transcript-integrity, Day 2 (standing hazard 1 confirmed on this day): a witness answer carries the JUDGE's label — the question "Agent Holt, you're able to watch that zoomed in version, is that right?" is answered "Yes, sir." under the "Judge" label. Also in this passage the witness's surname is rendered Hull / Hall / Holt within the same few turns; "Olsen" (Day 1) becomes "Olson" (Day 2); "Nester"/"Nestor" alternate; and victim's counsel appears as "Jeffrey Neiman" on Day 4 and "Jeff Nyman" on Day 5.

Transcript-integrity, Day 1 — corroborates CR-E05 §1.2 with two concrete instances in this exact passage. (a) The ruling sustaining the objection to 12.1 ("All right. I'm sustaining the objection...") carries a PROSECUTOR's label though its content is unmistakably the court's ruling. (b) In the end-of-day colloquy, DEFENCE counsel's turns carry the WITNESS's label ("David Hull": "Just a moment, Your Honor" in answer to "Does the defense want to be heard?"; "I mean, I made my objection already"; "we're happy to accommodate the state") interleaved with the witness's genuine in-court identification under the same label. Content-based reading is mandatory here; the labels are unusable.

A self-corrected date-range misstatement about 12.4. Asked what 12.4 depicts, the witness first answered that it was footage "for September 11th and September 12th." The State returned to it minutes later — "I may have misheard, but let's just be clear about this video" — and the re-elicited answer was "September 10th 2025, into the morning of the 11th 2025," which matches the Day-1 description of 12.1. Whether the first answer was a misspeak or a transcription artifact cannot be told from the text; the operative range in the record is 10 September into the morning of 11 September 2025.

The State's purpose for 12.1 was evidentiary, not presentational, and it paid off on redirect: the witness testified that on the zoomed version "it's apparent that Mr. Robinson, the individual jumping off the roof, is carrying an item," and later that "the zoomed version of the video makes it a lot clearer to see." This is the substantive reason the enhanced exhibit mattered, and it is a point that cuts in the State's favour on the Rule 403 non-cumulativeness argument the court rejected.

register_implications: D-52 RESOLVES, and narrowly. Resolution: the change in State's Exhibit 12.1's foundation between Day 1 and Day 2 was the creation and admission of State's Exhibit 12.4 — the same compilation with the alterations removed — followed by the witness's itemized sworn comparison of the two; State's Exhibit 12.3 was the identical, unamended statement throughout. Confidence High as to what happened; Medium-high as to the court's unstated reasoning for being satisfied. Evidence that would change it: the text of 12.3 itself, or a Day-2 filing showing a supplemental 1102 that never surfaced in the transcript.

D-52's resolution requires a correction-in-place in CR-E05 §5, in the ANALYST layer. The D-52 row's hypothesis ("most likely a revised or supplemental Rule 1102 statement, since ... the 12.3 admitted on Day 1 evidently did not [address the alterations], or the objection could not have succeeded") is refuted on two independent grounds — the Day-1 transcript shows the State quoting that very language from 12.3 before the ruling, and the court's stated ground for exclusion was the absence of a statement from whoever MADE the alterations, not silence about them. The section's own preceding paragraph already recorded the correct answer, so this is an internal inconsistency, not a sourcing failure. Supersession rows on both ends per the corrections rule.

CR-E04 §3 needs a cross-reference, not a correction: its 12.4 row ("the same compilation without circles, blurs or zooming") and its rulings paragraph are accurate, but a reader cannot tell that 12.4 exists BECAUSE 12.1 failed on Day 1. Its 12.3 row should also note that the court held that statement, standing alone, insufficient to authenticate the altered exhibit — 12.3 describes the alterations but does not account for them.

No analysis file in the library records this. This bears on CR-E03 (Days 2-3-5) and on any statement anywhere in the library that 12.1 "was admitted but not published."

Candidate for a new register entry or a §-level note: the court cited Rule 1102 as the foundation for admitting 12.4, where the foundation actually laid on the record for 12.4 was live sworn testimony. Soft — see the steelman in open items. Should not be opened as a discrepancy without the text of 12.3.

Bears on CR-ACQ §8 item 12 (Tier 1 acquisition of the surveillance exhibits) and on Q-11: the exhibit history of 12.1 now runs across four hearing days (excluded Day 1, admitted-not-published Day 2, reconsideration moved Day 4, published in courtroom Day 5), and any file describing it must date-stamp which ruling it is describing.

No new register entry is warranted for the witness's self-corrected date-range answer about 12.4 ("September 11th and September 12th" → "September 10th ... into the morning of the 11th"). It was corrected within the same examination and the corrected range matches Day 1. Record it as a recording-layer note in the Day-2 file, not as a discrepancy.

q52.both_directions: "WHAT CUTS FOR THE STATE. It did exactly what it told the court it would do, inside one evening, and did it the harder way: rather than papering the gap with a new statement, it built the unaltered comparator the court had asked for and put the comparison under oath, item by item — circles, blurs, zooms, each with a specific answer as to scope and effect. The defence did not contest any part of that itemization on cross-examination (scoped null 4). The State also volunteered against its own interest, telling the court unprompted that there is no footage of the shooting and clarifying exactly how close the video comes. Its practical claim — that the unenhanced version is genuinely hard to make out — was later independently echoed by counsel for the victim's family on Day 4, who told the court that the version played in open court \"was very hard for the family to view.\" The court's Rule 403 concern was needless repetition, not reliability; it received 12.1 in evidence and said it would review it in full in making the probable-cause determination. And the enhanced exhibit was ultimately shown in open court on Day 5, with the State not opposing. This is a correction running toward the State, and it should be logged as one: the overnight fix was substantive, not cosmetic.\n\nWHAT CUTS AGAINST THE STATE. The precise defect the court named on Day 1 was never literally cured. Nobody from the Utah County Attorney's Office testified; no Rule 1102 statement from whoever made the alterations was ever offered; the State's own Day-1 offer to call that person was not taken up. The State's stated ground for re-offering 12.1 was \"the foundation that was laid yesterday\" — that is, the same foundation the court had rejected the previous afternoon — and the court admitted the exhibit without addressing the renewed authenticity objection on the record at all. The gap was made immaterial by comparison rather than closed. Two further limits survive untouched by 12.4: both exhibits are selections, containing neither all the footage collected from UVU nor all the footage of the person believed to be Robinson, and no Rule 1102 statement in the record covers the selecting; and 12.4 is itself a compilation prepared by the same office, its foundation being one witness's testimony that it looks identical to raw footage he had reviewed. Finally, a note against over-hedging in the other direction: none of this makes the Day-2 admission irregular. A preliminary hearing tests probable cause, the magistrate is the fact finder, and reliable hearsay is admissible under Rule 1102. The point is only that the record shows what the court was given, and does not show what the court concluded from it."

q11_direct.headline: The author of the DNA reports the State put in evidence is an ATF forensic biologist called by the DEFENCE, and on direct she systematically stripped her own reports of everything they do not say: no source attribution, no verbal scale, no statement of how or when any DNA was deposited, DNA can appear on an item its contributor never touched — and on the swabs of the rifle bolts there was "support for inclusion" of Matthew Robinson, an elimination-sample donor identified in the question as the defendant's father, not a suspect. File read: ~/Documents/Kirk Robinson Research/files - Court record/CR-ACQ-2026-07-27_court-record-artifacts/prelim-hearing-transcripts/day5.txt, direct examination = L644–L2120.

findings.finding: Witness identity and qualifications, as stated by her: Caitlin Oliver (she spelled it O-L-I-V-E-R), employed by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives as a DNA Section Chief; Section Chief "since January" (NO YEAR STATED in the transcript); ~9 years with ATF; before that a forensic biologist; before ATF, a DNA analyst and DNA quality manager at Jefferson Parish Sheriff's Office, New Orleans, Louisiana. In September 2025 her duties were those of a forensic biologist, i.e. she was NOT a Section Chief when she did this work.

Assignment dates as she gave them: she agreed she received a request "around September 11th" to do DNA work at the request of the State of Utah; asked when she first received the assignment she said she would have to refer to her case record, was shown 'Oliver Three' page 3 for the witness only, and then said "September 12th, 2025", agreeing that was when she first started work. The September 12 date is memory-refreshed from a document, not independent recall.

Her laboratory's reporting scale, verbatim in substance: "We can come to five conclusions at our agency. So there can either be exclusion, limited support for exclusion, uninformative, limited support for inclusion, and support for inclusion." She confirmed her lab uses NO verbal qualifier scale (no 'strong', 'very strong'), because verbal scales "add subjective words to the front of this word support" and "the likelihood ratio statistic, the number stands on its own." This is a DIFFERENT convention from the FBI witness's scale that defence counsel referenced as prior testimony.

Counsel's reference at L815 to "a prior witness... from the FBI" who used a verbal support scale is functionally identifiable as Amanda Bakker, the FBI DNA Casework Unit forensic examiner (Quantico) called by the defence out of order on Day 2 — she spelled her name B-A-K-K-E-R on the record. Basis: she is the only FBI DNA examiner in the corpus; no other candidate appears.

DOJ Uniform Language for Testimony and Reports (ULTR): all three of her reports carry the standard conformity sentence — "Our reports adhere to the DOJ ULTR statement." Shown the document 'Exhibit Oliver Four' FOR THE WITNESS ONLY, expressly "Not admitted yet", titled by counsel as the Department of Justice Uniform Language for Testimony and Reports for Forensic Autosomal DNA Examination Using Probabilistic Genotyping Systems. Her account of what it requires: (1) if a verbal scale is used, use the one the document dictates, to unify language across DOJ laboratories; (2) "we cannot state that our evidence is infallible"; (3) "nor can we state that there is a inconclusive result" — clause (3) is a probable machine-transcript garble and should NOT be relied on as her words. She then agreed to counsel's propositions that the document bars asserting a zero error rate, bars asserting that a likelihood ratio of any magnitude provides absolute identification or source attribution, and bars 'reasonable degree of scientific certainty' language, and confirmed her reports comply.
findings.locator: day5.txt L855–L923 (Oliver Four introduced L871; garble at L883)

findings.finding: Her own uncoached formulation of the limit: "With forensic evidence, it's impossible to state with 100% certainty anything. That's why we report a likelihood ratio to speak to that uncertainty with a statistic."

Sample consumption. Her lab requires written permission-to-consume from the case agent (who is asked to consult an assigned attorney) before ANY work begins; the permission email in this case is at 'Oliver Three' page 15, shown for the witness only. Samples ENTIRELY CONSUMED in her analysis, read from Exhibit 30 page 8: 1.4, 1.6, 1.9, 1.10, 1.12, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1 and 5.1. Samples where DNA EXTRACTS WILL BE RETAINED: 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.5, 1.7, 1.8, 1.13, 7.1 and 8.1 — she confirmed these were swabs, that the swabs were consumed, and that only liquid extract remains for those. Her preservation policy as stated: "Where possible, we will not consume samples where it's possible" (transcript as written).

Counsel's split-sample premise — that the 1996 National Research Council recommendation was that samples be split at the front end so testing can be repeated, because "a wrongfully accused person's best insurance against a possibility of being falsely incriminated is the opportunity to have the testing repeated" — was READ BY COUNSEL and assented to by the witness ("Where possible, yes, that's correct" / "Correct"). The 1996 NRC content is counsel's characterisation, not the witness's independent recitation, and is unverified by this project — (checkable).

Mixtures: with the exception of the known samples from the known individual (single source), "the evidence samples were all mixtures"; she assented to counsel's "in many cases, they were mixtures of sometimes four and five people." She needed to consult her report tables (pages 2, 3 and 4) before answering.

The central limit, stated by her three separate times and never qualified: "None of the testing that I performed could speak to activity or what activity led to the deposition of the DNA" (L1107); "DNA can't speak to the activity that led to the deposition of the DNA" (L1339); "Once again, I cannot speak to the activity" (L1347). She agreed that major/minor contributor labels say nothing about activity, and agreed her results "cannot be interpreted as the analyst providing an opinion regarding who the source of the DNA is" — "we don't make source attribution statements. We will say there's support for inclusion, and then we back up that with a statistic."

She agreed that a media headline of the form 'Mr. Robinson's DNA is found on this item' would be a source attribution and "would not be scientifically defensible" — the question was counsel's; her answers were "Correct. Yes" and "Correct."

She REFUSED to accept the defence's framing of the NIST publication, an answer that cuts against the party calling her: "I don't know that I would call it a guidance document. NIST is not a regulatory body for DNA testing. It was a report that looked into forensic DNA reporting and specific human factors that could affect our testing. So, they may have had recommendations, but as far as them being a regulatory body that's issuing guidelines, I wouldn't state that."

Reporting cap: "for our likelihood ratio statistics, we cap the statistic at one trillion. The actual number could be a lot higher. It could be quintillion, octillion. We chose a trillion because it has meaning to people that can understand what a trillion is." She DECLINED to adopt the NIST rationale counsel read to her (that the cap reflects limitations of biostatistical modeling and independence assumptions of STR loci): "I believe we chose our cap for the reason I stated," and "I'm not familiar with the paper that's referenced there, so I would have to familiarize myself before I said I... agreed or disagreed." This is a second refusal to be led by the calling party.

Likelihood ratio and competing hypotheses, her own explanation: "a likelihood ratio of statistic compares the probability of the DNA profile of the evidence given two competing hypotheses or two competing scenarios. Typically, the first is that the person of interest is included and then the exclusionary hypothesis would be that the person of interest is excluded, so there's a random unknown unrelated individual contributing." She agreed that likelihood ratios "cannot speak to the likelihood of a proposition, only to the probability of the results given a pair of propositions," and that on that basis alone one cannot determine which proposition is most probable. She also agreed DNA statistics cannot imply uniqueness within a population.

Transfer and persistence, as she stated it. Pen example: an item handled successively by two people yields both profiles and "doesn't speak to who handled it last." Handshake-to-trigger example: asked whether counsel's DNA could end up on a gun trigger he touched after shaking her hand, without her ever touching the gun — "It is possible, yes" / "Yes." Persistence: "DNA is quite stable over time. It can be broken down due to environmental insults. So, things like heat and humidity are known to break down DNA over time, but I couldn't give you an exact number." Degradation: "There was degradation present in some of the samples." She also agreed with the read proposition that a profile may be developed even when the contributor never touched the item or area swabbed, and that a person's DNA may be present when they were not involved in the crime.

Elimination samples vs person-of-interest samples, her definition: "an elimination sample is a sample taken from a known individual that it may be assumed that they could have come into contact with it. If I were to, say, swab your vehicle, then I would want your DNA sample as an elimination to eliminate you in order to look for any additional DNA that may be there." Asked whether everyone in a house could contribute to a DNA result there, she answered only "It's possible" — she did NOT adopt counsel's stronger 'you would expect' framing.

MATERIAL GAP IN THE RECORD, from her own mouth: she requested elimination samples from the agents/investigators involved and DID NOT RECEIVE THEM. Her stated reason for requesting them: "The type of testing we perform is quite sensitive. So, it is a standard practice that we request elimination samples from any of the investigators involved in order to potentially eliminate them, in case they could have contaminated the evidence." The non-receipt was put by counsel ("you also requested, but I don't think you received") and confirmed "Correct."

Elimination-sample donors for items seized from the defendant's residence, as read by counsel from the document he called 'Oliver 157' and confirmed by her: Amber Robinson, Matthew Robinson, and Lance Twiggs, "because you had information that those people were associated with the house." She determined their DNA types and compared them to the evidence. NOTE: these three are living private individuals whose names entered open court solely as elimination donors, expressly not as suspects; no contact or location detail is recorded here.

Her results on the specific items counsel walked her through, in HER words, each time correcting counsel's looser phrasing: on item 1.4, which counsel called "a swab from the rifle" — "I would say there was support for inclusion of Matthew Robinson on the sample obtained from the swabs of the bolts of the rifle"; on 1.6 — "There is support for inclusion of Matthew Robinson"; on the swabs of the buttons of a Dremel tool (page 7) — support for inclusion of Lance Twiggs, "Correct"; and support for inclusion of Mr. Twiggs on other areas of the Dremel tool. She twice added the qualifier that a likelihood ratio statistic accompanies each such conclusion. Counsel's characterisation that he "found his DNA on that particular swab" was NOT adopted by the witness.

Q-50 GATED — RECORDED, NOT EXTENDED. Her household-transfer statement, in full and verbatim, given in answer to a question premised on Lance Twiggs living in the residence, contacting Tyler Robinson, and touching a Dremel button: "It's reasonable to assume that anyone living in the household could have contributed to DNA on an object found in that household." The formulation is expressly bounded twice — 'living in the household' and 'an object found in that household.' She was NOT asked about, and said nothing about, any item recovered away from the residence. Whether this reasoning reaches the towel or the screwdriver is a HUMAN-GATED question (Q-50) and is NOT answered here in either direction. Additional caution: the exchange concerns a living person who is not accused and who was granted use immunity (Day 3, Day 4).

Next-generation sequencing (NGS): she defined it as sequencing the individual bases, as against her own STR testing which measures length variation at highly variable repeat regions. She agreed NGS is "a newer technique" much discussed at seminars. ATF is NOT developing or using it — "Not at this time. No" — and has no plans to, "Not at this time. No." She believed some U.S. laboratories may use it but "wouldn't have direct knowledge of that." She used STRmix in this case, agreed it is sold by a New Zealand company, and was NOT aware of any STRmix NGS product: "I am not aware of NGS software" / "I was not aware. No." Asked whether NGS exists because sequences differ at equal lengths, she declined the premise and answered instead: "I think the reason for developing NGS software is to add another tool to a forensic biologist's tool belt" — a third refusal to be led.

Isoalleles, her own explanation before the objections landed: "there's something known as isoalleles. What that is is you may have, in this case, a 17 allele, but the sequence within that 17 allele is different. So, two people may have a 17, but they may have a different sequence within their 17 allele." She confirmed D3 is a location on the DNA strand, that Tyler Robinson had a 17 allele there, and that some of the evidence had a 17 allele at that location. She rejected counsel's 'number matching' shorthand: "it's not just number matching. We're using the STRmix software... We aren't using a chart and just doing number matching" — while agreeing that at bottom she compares alleles, measuring length only.

The isoallele/sequencing attack was CUT OFF and never became evidence. Three relevance objections by the prosecutor (functionally McBride, who then cross-examined) were SUSTAINED: on the 17A/17B/17C question (counsel withdrew and reframed), on the five-loci isoallele question, and on the 'would you exclude the person' question. The court's stated ground on the third: "as it relates to this witness and her firsthand knowledge, I'm not seeing that tie in as it relates to her." Defence counsel's proffer — "her testing cannot distinguish between these isoalleles, and therefore, it goes to the weight of the comparisons" and she is therefore "not in a position to draw conclusions" — is ARGUMENT OF COUNSEL only; the witness never adopted it and the court never accepted it. The State's answering proffer was that whether she could do sequencing is irrelevant to the analysis she did do.

Number-of-contributors line, including an internal tension in her own answers. She rejected the premise that the LR number varies with the assumed contributor count: "It's not necessarily the number of contributors... It could be a low number and be a single-source sample. It could be a high number and be a four-person mixture. It's not necessarily directly correlated with the number of contributors." Asked directly whether the final LR depends on the number of contributors assumed she said "No, it does not"; pressed with "It has no effect, whatsoever?" she then said "It can have an effect. It's possible." She agreed she uses "my training, education, and experience" to determine contributor number; confirmed "at least four/five contributors" signals it could be more; agreed difficulty of sorting increases with contributor number; and explained dropout in degraded profiles as why a single non-matching locus is not automatically an exclusion.

She AGREED with the NIST Mixture Study proposition read to her: "A likelihood ratio numeric value is not a measurement of the physical quantity" and "it is a ratio of probabilities in the opinion of the expert assessing the likelihood ratio and is dependent on the specific propositions used to formulate it and also on the individual making the assessment." Her answer: "Correct. Yes, I agree." This is the strongest defence-favourable concession in the direct and she gave it without qualification.

Final exchange of the direct: counsel put her own laboratory SOP (Exhibit Oliver 148, page 83) to her — that "assuming a mixture is a result of the combination of three people must be done with caution. For example, approximately 70% of four-person mixtures present as two- or three-person mixtures based solely on number of alleles present." She asked to see the SOP before answering; the State objected on probable-cause grounds and was OVERRULED (the only overruled objection of the direct); she confirmed counsel read it correctly, and to the closing question answered only "It's possible." Counsel then rested the direct: "Thank you. That's all I have."

EXHIBIT INVENTORY for the direct, with status exactly as the transcript gives it. (a) State's Exhibit 30 — Oliver's DNA report, "which is in evidence"; pages 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8 displayed; also called "Plaintiff's Exhibit 30" at L1063. (b) Exhibit Oliver Four — the DOJ ULTR document, "for the witness only... Not admitted yet" (L871). (c) Oliver Three — her case record/case notes, "for the witness only", page 3 (date received) and page 15 (permission-to-consume email), the latter again "for the witness only" (L943, L967). (d) Baker Exhibit 30 / "Baker-30" — the NIST publication 'Forensic DNA Interpretation and Human Factors', "for the witness only"; pages 135, 136, 137 (L1135, L1175). (e) Oliver 157 — "report number 157... which has been admitted" (L1464); pages 4, 5, 7 displayed. (f) Oliver 156 — the STRmix NGS product page; status NOT STATED (L1640). (g) 154 — the allele chart, "for the witness only" (L1688). (h) Exhibit Oliver 148 — her laboratory SOP, page 83; status NOT STATED (L2092). NOTHING was offered or admitted during the direct: a grep of day5.txt for offer/admit/receive-into-evidence/stipulate language returns no hit anywhere inside L644–L2120 other than descriptions of prior admissions.

HAZARD 3 REALISED INSIDE ONE WITNESS'S DIRECT: "Exhibit 30" designates two entirely different documents in the same examination — State's Exhibit 30 (Oliver's admitted DNA report) and "Baker Exhibit 30"/"Baker-30" (the NIST Forensic DNA Interpretation and Human Factors publication, witness-only). Any future citation MUST carry the party/series prefix. "Baker" is almost certainly the defence's BAKKER exhibit series: 'Baker' appears exactly twice in the whole five-day corpus, both here; the defence's Day 2 DNA witness spelled her name B-A-K-K-E-R; and defence counsel had just cited that FBI witness's verbal scale.
findings.locator: day5.txt L711, L1135, L1175; day2.txt L5133

findings.finding: EXHIBIT-NUMBERING SYSTEMS ARE NOT RECONCILED ON THE FACE OF THE RECORD. Three coexist: (i) State's exhibit numbers — the prosecutor said the already-admitted, already-published Oliver reports are "exhibits 30 and, I believe, 34" (his own hedge); (ii) spelled-out defence designations 'Oliver Three', 'Oliver Four'; (iii) three-digit numbers 148, 154, 156, 157. When defence counsel asked "What's the exhibit on this?" the answer from the bench area was "This is 154 in this application" — indicating the three-digit numbers may be DISPLAY-APPLICATION document IDs, not exhibit numbers. Yet counsel called 'Oliver 157' both "report number 157" and "admitted." This must not be silently harmonised.

TRANSCRIPT LACUNA at the start of the substantive DNA examination. A single counsel turn carries stream identifier 01:15:51 and its one-word answer carries 01:19:42, with no intervening turn; and the turn's text is internally discontinuous, fusing an exhibit-display request onto a mid-stream question: "Could we display State's Exhibit 30, which is in evidence? For instance, the next sample down, 1.2, where the state read paragraph D, admitted paragraph F..." The phrases "the next sample down" and "where the state read paragraph D" presuppose an earlier sample already discussed on this record, which does not appear. Material is omitted or collapsed here. (Per hazard 2 no duration or clock claim is made; the identifiers are cited as identifiers.) CONSEQUENCE: the single point in the ENTIRE direct where the witness assents to evidentiary support for the inclusion of Tyler Robinson on a named sample (1.2) sits at this seam and consists of the word "Correct."

REV SPEAKER LABELS FAIL ON DAY 5 IN AND AROUND THE OLIVER SEGMENT — four distinct failures. (1) The OATH ADMINISTRATION ("Do you solemnly swear that the testimony you shall give...") carries the label "Caitlin Oliver"; functionally it is the clerk or the bench, and the witness's first actual words are her name at L667. (2) At L2113 a WITNESS ANSWER ("It's possible") carries the label "Ms. Visser"; Ms. Visser is defence counsel — at L2600 she makes the record that Mr. Robinson was advised of and is declining his right to testify. (3) The MEDIA's substantive argument at L560–L567 carries the prosecutor's label "Mr. McBride": the bench had just said "Thank you. To the media," and the content is media advocacy ("Media is on board...", "let the parties go forward under the current procedures without further order or sanction"), whereas McBride elsewhere speaks unambiguously for the State ("The state has no rebuttal evidence to present at this hearing", L2588). (4) The bench is split across two labels, "Judge" (58 turns) and "Judge Graf" (22 turns), with no functional distinction; six turns are "Speaker X" and four are numbered speakers. Speakers in this segment must be identified functionally.
findings.locator: day5.txt L560–L567, L652–L655, L2113, L2597–L2604; label census across day5.txt

findings.finding: PROCEDURAL POSTURE BEFORE SHE WAS CALLED — the standing-objection colloquy, which the court never resolved. Grunander for the State pre-argued the probable-cause standard (citing State v. Schmidt, Pledger, Hester, Virgin, Droesbeke and Lopez) and said the State "may be lodging a standing objection of relevance and exceeding the scope," adding "The evidence is overwhelming. It's devastating." Burt for the defence answered that the State had already told the defence, after interviewing Ms. Oliver and the other experts, that there would be NO standing objection, and that it was therefore waived or estopped. THE COURT DID NOT RULE on waiver — it asked whether the media wished to be heard, was told no, and said "Mr. Burt, you may call your next witness." The State then lodged individual relevance objections during the isoallele line, expressly "invok[ing] Mr. Grunander's argument here and the case law that he referenced." Net effect: the pre-argument functioned as a standing objection without ever being ruled a standing objection.

The defence's stated purpose for calling her, recorded as a claim and NOT adopted: "the state presented DNA reports through a non-expert. They selectively read into the record a portion of those reports, which left an extremely misleading impression of the significance of that evidence. So I have the author of the report here and I'm going to hopefully educate the court on what the limitations are of the report." Related and independently notable: this is the DEFENCE calling the STATE's own report author as its witness, and the State conceding beforehand that her reports ("exhibits 30 and, I believe, 34") were already admitted and already published.

CONTEXT THAT CONSTRAINS THE EXHIBIT RECORD: the direct ran entirely under a sanction imposed that morning after the court found its order barring broadcast of Exhibit 16 had been violated — "members of the media shall no longer capture or broadcast any exhibits displayed by the parties during today's proceedings," extended in practice so that NO exhibits were displayed in the courtroom at all except on counsel's monitors. Victim's counsel objected that the family could not follow the evidence; the court adhered. This is why so much of the direct is counsel reading document text aloud and the witness assenting — the documents themselves were not on any public screen, and this transcript is the only public trace of their content.

The 1996 National Research Council split-sample recommendation and the quoted 'wrongfully accused person's best insurance' language were read by counsel, not recited by the witness (L999–L1007) — (checkable) against NRC II (1996).

Cross-examination (day5.txt L2133 onward) is Q-11 part 2 and is NOT covered here. It opens on accreditation (ISO 17025 plus FBI DNA standards) and runs to roughly L2580. Anything in the direct may be qualified there.

Coordinate with Q-06 (Amanda Bakker, Day 2): two DNA laboratories in this case — FBI and ATF — use DIFFERENT reporting conventions (FBI a verbal support scale, ATF a five-conclusion scheme with no verbal qualifiers). Whether and how the two reports were reconciled for the court is unexamined.

BEARS ON the Tier-1 acquisition roadmap: add (a) Oliver's three reports as filed exhibits, (b) the DOJ ULTR document, (c) the NIST 'Forensic DNA Interpretation and Human Factors' publication, (d) ATF DNA SOP page 83, (e) the exhibit list identifying State's 30/34 and the Oliver/Baker series. Five discrete, obtainable primary documents, four of them public.

DO NOT RESOLVE anything in this material against any named person. Every 'support for inclusion' statement recorded here is (i) a statement about a likelihood ratio, (ii) expressly not a source attribution by the witness's own testimony, and (iii) made at a probable-cause hearing at which no court has found any of this testimony true. Tyler Robinson is presumed innocent and, as of this reading, has not been bound over.

q11_direct.both_directions:
"CUTS FOR THE STATE. (1) The witness repeatedly declined to be led by the party that called her, and the pattern is consistent enough to be a credibility asset: she refused to call the NIST report a guidance document and volunteered that NIST 'is not a regulatory body for DNA testing' (L1155–L1159); she refused the NIST rationale for her lab's likelihood-ratio cap and said she was unfamiliar with the referenced paper rather than agreeing (L1227–L1243); she refused the premise that NGS exists because equal-length alleles differ in sequence, answering instead that it is 'another tool' (L1684); she refused counsel's 'number matching' description of her method (L1792); she refused counsel's 'you found his DNA on that swab' phrasing and restated it as 'support for inclusion' with an accompanying likelihood ratio (L1512, L1528); and where counsel's question carried a causal clause ('not because they were suspects, but because they were associated with the premises') she answered only 'There was support for inclusion of some of these individuals' (L1500). (2) Her report does contain evidentiary support for the inclusion of Tyler Robinson as a possible contributor on sample 1.2 and she confirmed it (L711/L715). (3) She confirmed Tyler Robinson has a 17 allele at D3 and that some evidence carried a 17 at that location (L1764–L1784). (4) She rejected the defence's core statistical premise outright — 'No, it does not' — that the final likelihood ratio depends on the assumed number of contributors (L1988). (5) The entire isoallele/NGS attack, the defence's most technically ambitious line, was excluded on three sustained relevance objections and never became evidence; counsel's proffer that her testing 'cannot distinguish between these isoalleles' is argument only, and the State's answer — that whether she COULD do sequencing is irrelevant to the analysis she DID do — went unrebutted (L1836–L1948). (6) She confirmed her laboratory is accredited to ISO 17025 and to the FBI's DNA standards (L2153, in cross). (7) Her cap is at one trillion 'the actual number could be a lot higher' — the reported statistic is deliberately understated, not overstated. (8) None of this is a probable-cause defence: as the State argued at length, at this stage the magistrate views evidence in the light most favourable to the prosecution and may not weigh it.

CUTS AGAINST THE STATE. (1) The most damaging testimony is not adversarial at all — it is the State's own report author explaining what her reports do not say: no source attribution ever, no verbal qualifier scale, no statement of how or when DNA was deposited, and a profile can be developed 'even when the contributor of that DNA never touched the item or area that was swabbed' (L1107, L1267, L1339, L1343). (2) Nine samples were entirely consumed — 1.4, 1.6, 1.9, 1.10, 1.12, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1, 5.1 — against her own lab's stated preservation policy and the split-sample principle she endorsed; for nine others only liquid extract remains (L1035–L1059). (3) She requested elimination samples from the investigating agents 'in case they could have contaminated the evidence' and DID NOT RECEIVE THEM (L1448–L1460); the contamination channel she herself identified was therefore never closed. (4) Support for inclusion of the defendant's father on the swabs of the rifle bolts and on item 1.6, and of Lance Twiggs on the Dremel buttons and elsewhere on the Dremel (L1512–L1560) — three household elimination donors appearing on the physical evidence, none of them suspects. (5) Mixtures of four and five contributors, 'at least' language signalling the number could be higher, and her own SOP's caution that approximately 70% of four-person mixtures present as two- or three-person mixtures on allele count alone, to which her answer was 'It's possible' (L1087, L2008, L2112). (6) Degradation was present in some samples and profiles can drop out (L1396, L1916). (7) She agreed without qualification that a likelihood ratio 'is a ratio of probabilities in the opinion of the expert... and also on the individual making the assessment' (L1980) — an expert concession that the number is not a measurement. (8) The defence's framing charge, that the State read a selective portion of these reports into the record through a non-expert (L631), is one the State never answered on the record in this segment.

A NOTE ON THE ASYMMETRY, so the audit trail does not read one way only: the strongest material against the State comes from the witness's affirmative answers, while the strongest material for the State comes from her REFUSALS — and refusals are easy to under-weight when summarising testimony, because they leave no quotable proposition behind. Six separate times she declined a defence framing. Any file built from this segment that reports only her concessions will be biased even if every quotation in it is accurate."

q11_close.headline: CR-ACQ §8 item 12 is answered and closable: State's Exhibit 12.1 — the enhanced (zoomed, circled) version of the UVU surveillance video — WAS played in open court in its entirety on Day 5 (2026-07-10), but courtroom-only: the court cut the livestream to audio for the duration and barred still photography of the monitors. The same session also closed the evidentiary phase of the preliminary hearing with NO bindover: defence rested, the State offered no rebuttal, Tyler Robinson declined to testify, and the matter was continued to 2026-09-01 at 10:00 a.m. for up to four hours of argument.

findings.finding: TARGET 1 — CR-ACQ §8 item 12 RESOLVED. State's Exhibit 12.1 was played in open court on Day 5 and the court announced its conclusion on the record. The Day-4 ruling had already GRANTED the request (the framing 'reserved at the close of Day 4' is imprecise: what the court reserved on Day 4 was the TIMING, not the decision). Day 4: the court granted 'that request' and said 'we will watch the totality of ... state's Exhibit 12.1', to be played 'at the conclusion of defense's presentation of evidence'. Day 5: the court readdressed that ruling in light of the morning's Exhibit 16 sanction, adhered to it, and the exhibit was played.

The operative Day 5 limits, stated verbatim in the ruling: (a) livestream TEMPORARILY LIMITED TO AUDIO ONLY while Exhibit 12.1 is displayed, on a least-restrictive-means finding; (b) Exhibit 12.1 'may be viewed by all persons physically present in the courtroom, including victim representative Ms. Kirk in her capacity as the victim representative'; (c) 'The same in court viewing rules applies to all parties and courtroom attendees.' The court then extended the limit orally beyond the written ruling: it also barred the STILL PHOTOGRAPHER — 'no still capture of any of the monitors during the publication of 12.1' — noting it had earlier only addressed video recording.

Mechanics of the playback as recorded: the court confirmed with the camera operator that the feed had been switched to audio-only BEFORE playing ('could the camera operator let me know when we're switched to an audio only? We are?'); the court confirmed with the State that Exhibit 12.1 has NO AUDIO TRACK; the court then directed play, and afterwards announced 'that concludes the playing of State's Exhibit 12.1. Video transmission may resume.' Neither party requested the benefit of the record afterwards.

Duration of the playback: approximately 10 minutes 23 seconds of recording-stream time elapses with no transcribed speech between the last timestamp before playback (02:27:55) and the next timestamped turn (02:38:18). This bracket is consistent with the Day-4 estimates ('about eight minutes' from victim's counsel; 'eight, give or take, two minutes' from the court). CAVEAT (hazard 2 and transcript integrity): Rev places the 02:27:55 marker immediately before the 'that concludes the playing' paragraph — only ~4 seconds after 'let's go ahead and play it now' — so the file's internal timestamping around the playback is self-inconsistent. The transcript alone cannot establish a duration; it establishes only the ~10m23s silent bracket.

WHAT EXHIBIT 12.1 IS (from Day 4, needed to make item 12 meaningful): State's Exhibit 12.1 is the ENHANCED version of the UVU surveillance video — described by victim's counsel as 'enhanced in that it was like zooming in and circles that were put on it'. State's Exhibit 12.4 is the UNMARKED, NON-ZOOMED version, which is the one that was approved for publication and played earlier. The court initially understood the request to cover only 'the portion that had been altered, which I believe is about one minute'; counsel corrected that and asked for 'the entirety of that exhibit', and the court granted the totality.

The Day 5 Exhibit 12.1 ruling is an EXPRESS CARVE-OUT from the sanction imposed that same morning. The court prefaced it: 'the court wishes to readdress yesterday's ruling in light of this morning's sanction as it relates to exhibit 16'. State's counsel had raised the matter unprompted before the break, and defence co-counsel (Rev label 'Chad Grunander') asked that a record be made with the livestream operators that 12.1 would not be published — which is what the audio-only order accomplished.

TARGET 2 — THE EXHIBIT 16 INCIDENT. The court made findings of fact on the record after reviewing the stream during a recess: State's Exhibit 24 was displayed on the monitor visible to the media camera; State's Exhibit 16 was displayed on ALL monitors and appeared on the livestream for approximately THREE AND ONE-HALF SECONDS; the camera operator redirected the camera BEFORE any party called attention to it; approximately 16 seconds later the court observed the image and interrupted. Both the State and the defence expressly accepted the court's recitation as accurate. (Exhibit content deliberately not reproduced here; the court characterised it as a 'note'.)

The court's own review MATERIALLY REVISED the parties' morning accounts in two directions — one worse for the media/State, one better. Worse: the exposure was ~3.5 seconds, not the 'approximately two seconds' the State's counsel had represented and media counsel had accepted ('I think the two seconds is about right'). Better: the camera operator moved off on her own initiative BEFORE anyone spoke, and the court did not notice until ~16 seconds later — whereas media counsel had described the court catching it contemporaneously ('at the time that was happening, the court also caught that'). The court had earlier told the State 'I find your representations to be accurate as to what occurred' before doing the review.

WHAT THE COURT SAID WAS ALREADY PUBLIC. Court's findings: the full text of Exhibit 16 'had previously been made public through a search warrant that was publicly available on or before April 2026'; the portion displayed did NOT contain the full note and consisted of approximately 78 words; approximately 15 of those words were included in the charging Information; and the full note had already been READ INTO THE RECORD during the preliminary hearing. Media counsel gave the underlying detail: the warrant was filed 17 September, held under seal six months as warrants often are, released in full on or about 16-17 March, with the full text at page seven — filed in the Fourth District 'but in a different court'.

THE SANCTION ACTUALLY IMPOSED. (1) Defence's primary request — reconsider and grant defence motion docketed at No. 305, excluding all electronic media coverage (video cameras, still photography, and audio) from all future proceedings — DENIED ('the analysis underlying the court's prior ruling remains unchanged'). (2) Defence's alternative — bar all cameras and electronic equipment from Day 5 — GRANTED IN PART AND DENIED IN PART: 'Effective immediately, members of the media shall no longer capture or broadcast any exhibits displayed by the parties during today's proceedings', found 'proportional and appropriate'. (3) As to the 1 September session: RESERVED — no EMC request had been filed and the court declined to pre-rule, inviting motions ahead of that hearing. The court expressly found its order prohibiting publication/broadcast of Exhibit 16 by the media camera WAS VIOLATED.

THE SANCTION'S PRACTICAL EFFECT WENT WELL BEYOND ITS WORDS — and this is not visible from the ruling text alone. In implementation, exhibits were displayed ONLY on counsel's monitors: the monitor to the court's right was off and the court confirmed 'This monitor is not on either. So it's only the attorneys.' Asked 'In the courtroom entirety?', the court answered 'As it stands right now, yes, that's correct.' Victim's counsel objected that 'it's just hard for the victim's family to be able to follow the evidence if everyone but the victim's family is able to view the exhibits here in court' and that presence without sight 'is not meaningful'; the court acknowledged the concern and declined to change the order. This is the direct reason the Exhibit 12.1 carve-out mattered at the close of the day.

The State proposed an alternative remedy that the court did NOT adopt: ordering the media to acquire a broadcast-delay capability (~30 seconds), the State reporting that media counsel had told it they 'do not have the capability to do that right now'. The word 'delay' appears nowhere in the court's ruling. The State also argued the defence had not timely objected when the exhibit was brought up during the examination, and that the coming witness (the DNA forensic biologist) carried lower risk because her reports — 'exhibits 30 and, I believe, 34' — had already been admitted and published.

HAZARD 1 — DAY 5 REV LABEL FAILURES ARE WORSE THAN 'fails less severely'. (a) The single label 'Mr. McBride' is applied to BOTH the prosecutor AND media-coalition counsel, including in immediately adjacent turns where the judge distinguishes them ('Turning to the state, and then to the media' → McBride; 'Thank you. To the media.' → McBride again, whose content is plainly media counsel: 'Appreciate the opportunity to be here to speak on behalf of the media'). (b) The OATH is labelled 'Caitlin Oliver' though it is the oath being administered TO her. (c) A witness answer is labelled 'Ms. Visser' (defence counsel) — content shows the witness answering Burt's SOP question. (d) The judge appears as 'Judge', 'Judge Graf', and (Day 4) 'Judge Tony F Graf Jr.' (e) Victim's counsel appears as 'Jeff Dyer' (9 hits) and 'Jeff Nyman' (1 hit) on Day 5 and 'Jeffrey Neiman' on Day 4 — three renderings, one speaker. Do not resolve any of these to a real person from Rev labels alone.

HAZARD 3 — A LIVE EXHIBIT-NUMBER COLLISION ON DAY 5. Defence exhibits carry a witness-name prefix: 'Oliver Three', 'Oliver Four', 'Oliver 148', '154', 'Oliver 156', 'Oliver 157', and 'Baker Exhibit 30'. 'Baker Exhibit 30' is the NIST publication 'Forensic DNA Interpretation and Human Factors'; 'State's Exhibit 30' (also called 'Plaintiff's 30') is Oliver's DNA report on the firearm. Both are referred to as 'Exhibit 30' within minutes of each other. Any citation must say which party's.

TRANSCRIPT INTEGRITY — an apparent ~3m51s untranscribed span inside Oliver's direct examination. Burt's turn is timestamped 01:15:51 and the witness's answering 'Correct' is timestamped 01:19:42, with the intervening turn reading as a splice ('Could we display State's Exhibit 30, which is in evidence? For instance, the next sample down, 1.2, where the state read paragraph D...'). Content is missing, not merely compressed. This is a Day 5 access-path caveat.

THE ISOALLELE LINE WAS SHUT DOWN, NOT ANSWERED. Defence counsel Burt asked whether researchers have found three variants at the D3 17 allele (17A/17B/17C) and whether isoalleles with different sequences but the same length occur at five loci of interest. The State objected on relevance to a probable-cause hearing, expressly invoking Grunander's earlier case-law argument; the court SUSTAINED, twice, and sustained a third related question on the ground that it did not tie to this witness's firsthand knowledge ('as it relates to this witness and her firsthand knowledge, I'm not seeing that tie in'). Burt's stated theory of relevance: 'her testing cannot distinguish between these isoalleles, and therefore, it goes to the weight of the comparisons.' The witness DID define isoalleles before the objection landed, but never answered whether 17A/B/C exist or whether sequence differences across loci would produce an exclusion.

Cross-day link on isoalleles: the term appears in only two of the five days — day2.txt (3 hits, at least one in a witness Rev labels 'Ms. Bakker', the FBI examiner) and day5.txt (3 hits, Oliver). Days 1, 3 and 4 have zero. The defence ran the same methodological line at two different laboratories' witnesses.

STATE'S CROSS-EXAMINATION OF OLIVER (she was the DEFENCE's witness; the defence called the State's own ATF analyst). The State established: ATF lab accredited to ISO 17025 and to FBI DNA-specific standards; accreditation requires validated methodologies; methods 'accepted by courts across the country'; competency testing before casework and twice-yearly proficiency testing, satisfied both currently and at the time of this testing. Then, from State's Exhibit 30, the locations on the firearm with evidentiary support for inclusion of Tyler Robinson: swabs of the stock and grips; butt plate; trigger and trigger guard (possible ridge detail/smudging); bolt (possible ridge detail/smudging); fore-end; barrel (possible ridge detail/smudging); possible ridge detail/smudging on the optical accessory; the protected underside of the receiver after disassembly; one .30-06 cartridge case; and two .30-06 cartridges.

THE TWO LIKELIHOOD-RATIO CALCULATIONS THE STATE ELICITED. Calculation 3 — item 1.3, swabs of the trigger and trigger guard: the DNA profile is 'at least one trillion times more likely if it originated from Tyler Robinson as the major component and three unknown unrelated individuals than if it originated from four unrelated individuals'; paragraph E probability statistic: less than one in a trillion. Calculation 7 — items 1.13 (protected underside of the receiver after disassembly) and 2.1 (one .30-06 cartridge case), grouped because both were two-person mixtures yielding the same magnitude, NOT because they were tested together: 'at least one trillion times more likely if they originated from Tyler Robinson as the major contributor and an unknown unrelated individual than if they originated from two unknown unrelated individuals'; same <1-in-a-trillion probability statistic. Both numbers are floor values: the lab caps reporting at one trillion and 'would not report a number higher than one trillion'.

DEFENCE REDIRECT — the concessions that follow the trillion figures. On item 1.3 (trigger/trigger guard): the trigger and trigger guard were swabbed TOGETHER, so the analyst 'wouldn't be able to say where the DNA came from'; there were signs of degradation in that sample; asked whether the major profile had the LARGEST amount of degradation, the answer was 'There was... Yes'; the sample is consistent with AT LEAST four contributors and could be five, six or seven, the minor contributors being unsuitable for comparison 'due to that complexity'; the analyst did not perform the swabbing herself. On item 1.1 (swabs of the stock): a mixture of four individuals with TWO major contributors. Across all samples: no way of knowing when or how the DNA was deposited; 'major/minor' reflects quantity of DNA only, never activity; the paragraph-E statistic is a restatement of the likelihood ratio and carries the same limitations — no source attribution, no infallibility, no zero error rate.

SAMPLE CONSUMPTION — a cross-reference the State's cross did not surface. Entirely consumed: items 1.4, 1.6, 1.9, 1.10, 1.12, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1 and 5.1. DNA extracts retained (swabs consumed, liquid extract remaining): 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.5, 1.7, 1.8, 1.13, 7.1 and 8.1. Item 2.1 — one of the two items carrying the trillion-order likelihood ratio in calculation 7 — is on the ENTIRELY CONSUMED list. The witness agreed the split-sample policy traces to the 1996 National Research Council recommendation that samples be split where feasible because 'a wrongfully accused person's best insurance against a possibility of being falsely incriminated is the opportunity to have the testing repeated'.

ELIMINATION SAMPLES. Requested in connection with items seized from the residence: Amber Robinson, Matthew Robinson and Lance Twiggs. Results as testified: support for inclusion of Matthew Robinson on the sample from swabs of the bolt(s) of the rifle (item 1.4) and again on item 1.6; support for inclusion of Lance Twiggs on swabs of the buttons of a Dremel tool and on other areas of the Dremel. The witness twice corrected counsel's 'you found his DNA' to 'there was support for inclusion', with a likelihood ratio attached, and framed the results neutrally: 'It's reasonable to assume that anyone living in the household could have contributed to DNA on an object found in that household.' Separately: elimination samples were requested from the AGENTS involved in the case — standard practice because 'the type of testing we perform is quite sensitive' — and were NOT received.

OPEN ITEM — a bolt-swab identity question the transcript does not settle. In the report Burt called 'Oliver 157', item 1.4 is 'the swabs of the bolts of the rifle' and carries support for inclusion of Matthew Robinson. In State's Exhibit 30, 'the swabs of the bolt of the rifle with possible ridge detail/smudging' is listed among the locations with evidentiary support for inclusion of Tyler Robinson. Whether these are the same physical swab item, or differently-numbered items across two of the three reports, is NOT established on the face of the transcript. Do not merge them.

WHY THE DEFENCE CALLED THE STATE'S ANALYST — Burt's stated purpose on the record: 'the state presented DNA reports through a non-expert. They selectively read into the record a portion of those reports, which left an extremely misleading impression of the significance of that evidence. So I have the author of the report here and I'm going to hopefully educate the court on what the limitations are of the report.' He also argued the State had WAIVED or was estopped from a standing objection, because after interviewing Oliver and the other experts the State had told the defence there would be no standing objection — which is why a pre-scheduled ruling hearing was not needed and why witnesses were flown from the East Coast.

THE STATE'S PROBABLE-CAUSE ARGUMENT, on the record and unrebutted on the merits. Prosecutor Grunander recited the magistrate's standard with six Utah citations: State v. Schmidt (reasonable inferences cutting both ways must go to the fact finder), State v. Pledger (Utah 1995) (the standard bars requiring the prosecution to eliminate alternative inferences), State v. Hester (Utah App. 2000) (the magistrate 'may not sift or weigh the evidence'), State v. Virgin (Utah 2006) (evidence may be disregarded only if 'so contradictory, inconsistent, or unbelievable'), State v. Droesbeke (Utah App. 2010), and State v. Lopez (Utah 2020) ('Under this low bar, it may be difficult for the defense to overcome a prima facie showing of probable cause'). He framed it as notice of a likely standing objection rather than the objection itself, and characterised the record as 'The evidence is overwhelming. It's devastating.'

CLOSE OF THE HEARING — the posture as of the end of Day 5. Defence: 'we have no further witnesses, Your Honor.' State: 'We have no rebuttal evidence to present at this hearing.' Defence counsel (Rev label 'Ms. Visser') made a record that Robinson had been advised of his right to testify and was choosing not to; the court confirmed and noted he was 'nodding in the affirmative'. The preliminary hearing was CONTINUED to 1 September at 10:00 a.m. for an IN-PERSON hearing, with up to FOUR HOURS TOTAL allocated for argument encompassing both parties; the defence requested that Robinson be physically present and the court so ordered. The proceeding was adjourned without any probable-cause determination.

Two contextual items from the Day 5 openings that bear on the case posture generally: the court's standing decorum order as read includes a prohibition on spectators 'expressing any position concerning the status of this case as a capital offense'; and the court conducts a NAMED, ON-THE-RECORD COLLOQUY with the media camera operators every morning, confirming they have reviewed the decorum order and can comply. Defence counsel's sanction argument rested squarely on that daily colloquy ('every morning this court has a colloquy with the camera operators about their ability to comply').

Defence's aggravating argument, twice made and not disputed by the court: this was the SECOND violation of the court's electronic-media orders — 'We had earlier proceedings in this case where the cameras depicted images inside the courtroom that the court had prohibited and the court imposed certain consequences on the media as a result of that.' Media counsel implicitly corroborated the prior incident ('a time when the camera was placed in a location in the courtroom that was causing challenges. The court moved it'). Defence framing: 'I'm a baseball fan, and I just don't think the court needs to wait for the third strike.' The court's ruling did not adopt or reject the second-strike characterisation in terms.

q11_close.both_directions:
"CUTS FOR THE STATE. (1) The State's cross of the defence's own witness produced the strongest DNA figures in the record: likelihood ratios of at least one trillion — a reported floor, not a ceiling, because the lab caps at one trillion — supporting inclusion of Tyler Robinson as the major component on the trigger/trigger-guard swabs, on the protected underside of the receiver after disassembly, and on a FIRED .30-06 cartridge case; plus a list of nine or more locations across the rifle with evidentiary support for inclusion. (2) The witness confirmed lab accreditation (ISO 17025 plus FBI DNA standards), validated methodologies, methods 'accepted by courts across the country', and her own satisfaction of competency and proficiency standards both currently and at the time of testing. (3) The court sustained the State's relevance objections three times, confining the defence's isoallele/NGS attack, and expressly agreed with the State's framing that the witness's inability to do sequencing does not bear on the analysis she did do. (4) The State's probable-cause authorities (Schmidt, Pledger, Hester, Virgin, Droesbeke, Lopez) went into the record unrebutted on the merits, and the court's own conduct — sustaining on 'this is a probable cause hearing' grounds — tracks them. (5) On the media incident, the court's findings were substantially favourable to the State's position on prejudice: brief exposure, operator self-correction before anyone spoke, the full text already public through an unsealed search warrant, ~15 of the displayed words already in the Information, and the whole note already read into the record. (6) The court DENIED the defence's principal sanction (motion 305) and granted the victim representative's Exhibit 12.1 request over a standing defence objection.

CUTS AGAINST THE STATE. (1) The State's own analyst gave the defence every limitation it asked for: no source attribution at any likelihood-ratio magnitude, no statement of infallibility or zero error rate, no 'reasonable degree of scientific certainty', no inference about activity, mechanism, or timing of deposition, and agreement that 'the true number of contributors of DNA to an item can never be known'. She agreed a profile can develop where the contributor never touched the item, and that 'major contributor' is a quantity label carrying no behavioural meaning. (2) The trigger/trigger-guard sample — one of the trillion-LR items — was swabbed as trigger AND guard together, showed degradation, was consistent with AT LEAST four contributors (possibly five, six or seven), and its major profile carried the largest degradation. (3) Household members produced inclusion support on case items: the father on rifle-bolt swabs and on item 1.6; the roommate on the Dremel — the transfer/association mechanism the defence needs, established through the State's analyst. (4) Elimination samples were requested from the investigating agents and were NOT received, leaving investigator contamination unexcluded by the lab's own standard practice. (5) Nine items were ENTIRELY CONSUMED — including item 2.1, one of the two items in the trillion-order calculation 7 — foreclosing the independent re-testing the 1996 NRC recommendation contemplates. (6) The court found the State's/media's conduct VIOLATED its order, and it was the prosecutor who was examining and whose paralegal had the exhibit up when it reached the livestream; a sanction was imposed and the court declined to say it would not go further on 1 September. (7) The defence's characterisation that the State had presented the DNA reports through a non-expert and read them selectively stands on the record without a State rebuttal, and the State called no rebuttal evidence at all.

CUTS AGAINST BOTH / NEUTRAL. The court's post-recess review corrected the record in one direction against the media (2 seconds became 3.5) and in one direction in its favour (the operator moved off unprompted, and the court did not notice for ~16 seconds — meaning the bench's own contemporaneous impression, which it had already endorsed as accurate, was wrong). The transcript itself is a defective witness in two places on Day 5 — a ~3m51s untranscribed span in the direct and a self-inconsistent timestamp bracket around the Exhibit 12.1 playback — and both of those cut against confident use of Day 5 by either side."

q06_a.headline: Both headline DNA statistics — 1.7 octillion (Item 7-1, towel) and 30 quintillion (Item 8-1, screwdriver handle) — are ratios between two hypotheses that BOTH assume Lance Twiggs is one of exactly two contributors; the only variable is whether the second contributor is T. Robinson or an unknown unrelated person. FBI examiner Amanda Bakker testified on direct that the STRmix run comparing Twiggs alone to Item 7-1 returned a likelihood ratio of ONE, which she classified as "uninformative," and that she did not use that calculation to place Twiggs in the sample — she assumed him visually, because "the field submitted him as an elimination." The conditioning that carries both octillion/quintillion figures therefore rests on investigator instruction plus the examiner's visual read, not on a statistically supportive likelihood ratio.

findings.finding: Name spelled on the record by the witness herself: "My name is Amanda Bakker. My last name is spelled B-A-K-K-E-R." The transcript thereafter alternates between "Ms. Bakker" and "Ms. Baker," and the defence exhibit series is captioned "Bakker 7" once (L5457/L5461) and "Baker 4 / Baker 34 / Baker 35 / Baker 38" everywhere after. These are one witness and one exhibit series.

Employer and role as stated on direct: "I am a forensic examiner in the DNA Casework Unit of the FBI laboratory located in Quantico, Virginia," a DNA analyst there "a little more than 10 years." Her duties: review case information and evidence, decide which items are tested and which tests are performed, write an "exam plan" (a to-do list for the biologist), review the data, draw conclusions in a report, and testify.

NO qualifications, education, accreditation, training or proficiency evidence was elicited during the ENTIRE defence direct beyond the two sentences above. Her B.S. in biology (Salisbury University), ~1.5 years as an FBI contractor on the Federal Convicted Offender Program, ~6 years as a DNA Casework Unit biologist, appointment as forensic examiner in 2015, ANAB accreditation, the two-year training programme with oral/written boards and moot court, the competency exam, 8 hours annual continuing education, and vendor proficiency testing were ALL elicited by the STATE on cross-examination. She was never formally tendered or qualified as an expert on the record.

findings.finding: What the State of Utah requested is NOT specified anywhere on the direct record. The full exchange is: Q "in this case, were you requested by the state of Utah to do certain testing?" A "Yes, I was." No scope, no item list, no test type. She separately testified that SHE determines which items are tested and which tests are performed. Timing: called upon September 2025; "I believe we received evidence the first time was September 11th of 2025."

Turnaround and priority: normal FBI DNA Casework Unit turnaround "wavered between 90 days and over 200 days… on average, it's somewhere between 180 and 200 days." This case came in at "Priority 1 Level" — "we worked 24 hours a day, seven days a week until examinations were complete." Testing began while evidence was still being inventoried, because of "the high profile nature of this case."

COMMUNICATION LOG, 13 September 2025 (case-file page 22, read into the record by the witness): she told FBI SA Folger and Utah SBI SA Dave Hull the "technically reviewed results that Robinson was included as a possible contributor to the DNA from the towel and the screwdriver," that both agreed no additional immediate comparisons were needed, and that all remaining comparisons would be in the laboratory report. She confirmed "possible contributor" was the language required by FBI reporting standards.

State's Exhibit 31 is Bakker's laboratory report dated 15 September 2025, six pages, ALREADY ADMITTED AND PUBLISHED before she took the stand (admitted at L4777 during Faumuina). Defence referred to it as "our Tab 2." Her report conforms to the DOJ Uniform Language for Testimony and Reports for Forensic DNA Examinations.

EXHIBIT STATUS — Defence Exhibit Bakker 7: "Approved Standards for Scientific Testimony and Reports for Autosomal DNA Testing" (FBI, 6 pages). Shown to the witness only, then ADMITTED over the State's relevance objection and PUBLISHED to courtroom, monitor and camera. The defence organises its exhibits by witness under "Named Witnesses."

EXHIBIT STATUS — the DOJ document "Uniform Language for Testimony and Reports for Forensic Autosomal DNA Examinations Using Probabilistic Genotyping Systems" (defence Tab 8) was displayed TO THE WITNESS ONLY ("No, not on the big screen… This is just for the witness") and was NEVER moved into evidence or admitted anywhere in day2.txt. On cross the prosecutor nonetheless referred to it as "an Exhibit 8.4, Baker 8.4." Two substantive policy provisions were read from it into the record from an unadmitted document.
